title: Forgetting, false memory and smart study
note: Forgetting is fast at first and then levels off, and remembering is reconstruction, not replay. The best-supported study methods use this: retrieval practice (testing yourself), spacing sessions over time, and interleaving problem types. They feel harder than rereading, but they produce more durable learning.

read.title: Study the way memory works
text: Most students study by rereading and highlighting. These feel productive because the material grows familiar, but familiarity is not the same as being able to produce an answer on your own. Research points to methods that feel harder and work better.

The first is retrieval practice. Each time you pull an answer out of memory, you make it easier to retrieve the next time. Flashcards, practice questions, and explaining a topic from memory all count. Tests are not just measurements; they change what you remember.

The second is spacing. Studying the same material in several shorter sessions spread over days beats one long session, even when total time is equal. A little forgetting between sessions makes the next retrieval effortful, and that effort strengthens the memory.
The third is interleaving: mixing problem types instead of doing a block of one kind. Mixed practice forces you to decide which method fits each problem, the same choice a real test demands.

Each of these is a desirable difficulty. Progress can feel slower, but what you learn lasts longer. Check yourself often, so your sense of what you know stays honest, and sleep after studying, since sleep helps consolidate new memories.

q.q: Why can rereading give a false sense of mastery?
o: It makes material familiar without practicing recall
